Hi Maria — thanks for the heads up and for sharing the snapshot. We can absolutely support a short-duration uplift, and I outlined two practical paths below (short and middling emails so procurement has concrete options):

Option A — Transient Headroom (fastest)
- Temporary uplift to peak QPS for a defined window (you pick start/end)
- Billing: prorated pay-as-you-go for tokens consumed during the window at our standard on-demand rate
- Safeguard: we can place a hard dollar cap you set to prevent runaway charges
- Timing: we can enable this within 24 hours if we have authorization from procurement

Option B — Short Commit + Overrun Credit (recommended if you expect to convert to longer-term)
- Short-term commit for the uplift (e.g., 3 weeks / fixed additional committed capacity)
- Discount: 15% off on the incremental commit for the commit period
- Overrun true-up: any usage above the short commit is billed at on-demand, but we will credit 50% of overrun (applied to the next invoice) if you sign the commit within 7 days of the uplift

We usually see customers pick Option B when they want a predictable effective rate and a runway to convert the uplift into a sustained commit. If you need a stricter cap, we can add a per-token soft ceiling with alerts + automatic throttle fallback if the ceiling is reached.

Next steps I propose:
1) You confirm exact uplift window (start/end timestamps) and an initial dollar cap if you want one.
2) I’ll schedule a 20-minute alignment call with Ben (billing) and Grace (launch support) and drop a one-page amendment for your procurement to review.

If procurement can share a PO stub now, we’ll fast-track the amendment and enable the uplift once authorized.

On the logistics side, can you also tell us expected peak RPS and percent of requests that need streaming vs non-streaming responses? That affects our runtime allocation.

—Jonas
Jonas Weber
